core_semantic_distinctions.meaning: An ion has nonzero net charge because proton and electron counts differ; a neutral atom/molecule has net charge zero.
Cations have fewer electrons than protons; anions have more electrons than protons.
The distinction concerns number of constituent atoms, independent of charge sign.
Net ionic charge and formal oxidation state are not interchangeable for general polyatomic systems.
The source explicitly distinguishes spectroscopic Fe I/II/III nomenclature from oxidation-state notation.
Ionization concerns formation of charged species by electron gain/loss; dissolution releases ions from an ionic solid into a solvent.
Water can directly form solvation shells; the source describes a distinct amphiphile-mediated mechanism in nonpolar liquids.
An ion pair is a coupled product of a physical ionization event, while an individual ion is a charged chemical entity.
Radiation can generate ion pairs in gases, whereas electrochemical processes can create or move ions through conducting media.

claims.statement: An ion is an atom or molecule with a net electrical charge because its total number of electrons is unequal to its total number of protons.
Net ionic charge in units of elementary charge equals the number of protons minus the number of electrons.
Ions are divided into cations/anions and monatomic/polyatomic ions according to charge and atomic composition.
Ion charge is written as a superscript to the right of the chemical formula; magnitude is written before sign for charges greater than one and omitted for singly charged species.
Physical ionization in a fluid can create an ion pair consisting of a free electron and a positive ion.
The term ion was introduced by Michael Faraday in 1834 after William Whewell suggested terminology; the names reflect motion toward oppositely charged electrodes.
Arrhenius proposed that crystalline salts dissociate into charged particles in solution and that free ions exist even without an applied electric current.
Ions in liquids or released from solids can acquire solvation shells; solvent interaction stabilizes separated ions through combined energy and entropy effects.
Charged ions are attracted to opposite charges, repelled by like charges, and can have trajectories deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
Electron-cloud differences make anions larger and cations smaller than their corresponding neutral atoms or molecules; H+ is a bare proton.
Ions occur widely in nature, including seawater and the ionosphere, and metal ions can influence gemstone color through light absorption.
Ion sources and ions are used in mass spectrometry, optical emission spectroscopy, particle acceleration, ion implantation, ion propulsion and other technologies.
Ionic gradients across biological membranes participate in signaling and metabolism; disruption can contribute to cell death.
Ionization of gas by alpha, beta, gamma and X-ray radiation produces ion pairs that can be detected with ionization chambers and amplified with avalanche detectors.
Roman numerals in chemical oxidation-state notation and spectroscopic ion notation do not have the same semantics; spectroscopic Fe I denotes neutral Fe while Fe II denotes Fe+.
Monatomic ions form by gain or loss of valence-shell electrons; inner-shell electrons generally do not participate in ordinary chemical ion formation.
Sodium tends to lose its valence electron and chlorine tends to gain one, producing Na+ and Cl−; opposite charges then form NaCl.
Polyatomic ions commonly form by gaining or losing elemental ions such as H+; protonation of NH3 produces NH4+.

Ionization in low-dielectric nonpolar liquids can occur when amphiphilic solutes provide both a polar head for dissociation and a hydrophobic tail for solubility; neutral solute molecules can form a self-solvation layer.
Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron, and successive ionization energies rise markedly after an orbital block is exhausted.
Ionic bonding results from attraction of oppositely charged ions, which generally form ionic compounds and crystal lattices rather than existing independently.
The source enumerates common monatomic cations, polyatomic cations, monatomic anions and polyatomic/oxo/organic-acid anions.
